questions.subject: History
questions.text: The pre-colonial kingdom of Ife occupies a central place in Yoruba tradition mainly because it is regarded as the
options: capital of the Kwararafa Kingdom
seat of the Sokoto Caliphate
cradle of Yoruba civilisation and the origin point of Yoruba kingship
principal centre of the trans-Saharan salt trade
questions.explanation: Yoruba oral tradition holds Ife to be the site of creation and the source from which Yoruba dynastic rulers, including the Alaafin of Oyo, trace their descent.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Benin Kingdom's political structure under the Oba was distinctive in pre-colonial Nigeria for its
options: administration entirely through Islamic emirs
elaborate palace bureaucracy of title-holding chiefs organised into distinct societies
complete absence of any central authority
governance by a rotating council with no single ruler
questions.explanation: Benin's monarchy was supported by a sophisticated system of palace and town chiefs grouped into societies such as the Uzama, Eghaevbo n'Ogbe and Eghaevbo n'Ore, which advised and served the Oba.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: Among the Igbo of south-eastern Nigeria before 1800, political authority was most typically vested in
options: a council of European trade agents
a hereditary emperor ruling from a fixed capital
village assemblies, age-grades and title societies rather than a single monarch
an Islamic caliph appointed by Sokoto
questions.explanation: Much of Igbo society was organised on a segmentary, republican basis, with decisions made through village assemblies, age-grade associations and title-taking societies instead of centralised kingship.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Nupe Kingdom, located along the Niger River, developed a centralised monarchy under a ruler whose title was the
options: Attah of Igala
Obi of Onitsha
Amanyanabo
Etsu Nupe
questions.explanation: The Nupe Kingdom was governed by a centralised monarch known as the Etsu Nupe, based around the Niger-Kaduna confluence area.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The city-states of the eastern Niger Delta, such as Bonny and Kalabari, based their political and economic power chiefly on their control of
options: salt mines located deep in the delta swamps
large cavalry forces used to raid neighbouring savanna states
trans-Saharan caravan routes to North Africa
waterborne trade routes linking the interior to European merchants on the coast
questions.explanation: Delta states such as Bonny and Kalabari prospered as middlemen, using canoe houses to control trade between interior producers and European ships anchored at the coast.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Kano Chronicle is an important historical source mainly because it
options: records the treaty ending the Yoruba civil wars
records a detailed king-list and history of the Hausa state of Kano
was the founding legal code of the Sokoto Caliphate
documents the arrival of the first British explorers in Nigeria
questions.explanation: The Kano Chronicle is a valuable indigenous written source listing the rulers of Kano and major events in the kingdom's history before the colonial period.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: Trans-Saharan trade linked the Hausa states and Kanem-Bornu to North Africa chiefly through the exchange of
options: cocoa and rubber for European manufactured cloth
crude oil for European currency
palm oil for British firearms
salt, cloth and slaves for goods such as horses, weapons and luxury items
questions.explanation: Long before European contact on the coast, northern Nigerian states traded across the Sahara, exchanging local goods and slaves for salt, horses, weapons and other imports from North Africa.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The spread of Islam into the Hausa states before 1800 came largely through the activities of
options: Wangarawa (Mande) traders and clerics travelling along trans-Saharan trade routes
British Christian missionaries based in Lagos
Portuguese explorers sailing along the West African coast
Fulani jihadists after 1804
questions.explanation: Islam reached the Hausa states well before the nineteenth-century jihad, introduced gradually from around the fourteenth century by Wangarawa traders and clerics moving along Saharan trade networks.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Aro of south-eastern Nigeria extended their influence over neighbouring Igbo communities mainly through
options: alliance with Portuguese slave traders on the coast
military conquest using cavalry forces
direct rule imposed by a centralised Aro monarchy
control of the Ibiniukpabi (Long Juju) oracle and dominance of regional trade networks
questions.explanation: The Aro built a wide-reaching network of influence not through conquest but through the religious authority of the Arochukwu oracle and their control of trade and settlement diaspora.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Efik of Old Calabar rose to prominence in the era of Atlantic trade mainly as
options: a cavalry-based military power dominating the eastern Niger Delta
producers of cloth exported directly to Europe
middlemen who supplied European traders with slaves and later palm produce from the interior
converts who introduced Islam to south-eastern Nigeria
questions.explanation: The Efik city-states of Old Calabar became wealthy as intermediaries, channelling captives and, later, palm produce from the interior to European ships along the Cross River.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: Which of the following best describes the political organisation of the Tiv people before 1800?
options: A centralised monarchy modelled on Benin
A decentralised system based on lineage segments rather than a central king
A confederation governed by warrant chiefs
An Islamic emirate under a Sarki
questions.explanation: The Tiv, like many Middle Belt groups, organised society around segmentary lineage structures and had no tradition of centralised kingship before colonial rule.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Oyomesi council in the Old Oyo Empire held the constitutional power to
options: negotiate treaties directly with European powers
compel an unpopular Alaafin to commit suicide by presenting him with an empty calabash or parrot's eggs
select the Oba of Benin
appoint the Emir of Sokoto
questions.explanation: As a check on royal power, the Oyomesi could signal loss of confidence in the Alaafin by presenting him with an empty calabash or parrot's eggs, compelling him to take his own life.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The military strength of the Old Oyo Empire at its height was based significantly on its
options: alliance with the Sokoto Caliphate
extensive use of firearms purchased from North Africa
large and effective cavalry force suited to the northern savanna terrain
powerful navy controlling the Atlantic coastline
questions.explanation: Old Oyo's location in open savanna country allowed it to build a formidable cavalry, which was central to its military dominance over much of Yorubaland.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: Before 1800, the Kanem-Bornu Empire's long survival as a major state was aided chiefly by its
options: alliance with Portuguese traders on the Atlantic coast
conversion of its population to Christianity
isolation from all neighbouring states and trade networks
strategic control of trans-Saharan trade routes near Lake Chad and adaptable political institutions
questions.explanation: Kanem-Bornu's location athwart key trans-Saharan trade routes, combined with resilient political and military institutions, allowed it to remain a major power for many centuries.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: Which of the following statements best characterises the diversity of pre-colonial political systems in the Nigeria area up to 1800?
options: They were uniformly organised as Islamic emirates
They had no organised political institutions of any kind
They were all directly modelled on the government of Old Oyo
They ranged from highly centralised monarchies to decentralised, lineage-based societies
questions.explanation: The pre-colonial Nigeria area contained a wide spectrum of political forms, from centralised states like Benin, Oyo and the Hausa kingdoms to decentralised societies such as the Igbo and Tiv.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Idoma and Igala peoples of the Niger-Benue confluence area both trace elements of their traditional political culture to influence from the
options: Benin Kingdom, particularly in aspects of court titles and ritual kingship
Portuguese trading forts on the coast
Kanem-Bornu Empire
Sokoto Caliphate's emirate system
questions.explanation: Oral traditions and shared court practices link the ruling institutions of the Igala and related confluence peoples to historical influence from Benin, especially in royal titles and rituals.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The introduction of new food crops such as maize and cassava into the Nigeria area before 1800 came mainly through contact via the
options: Sokoto Jihad's northern conquests
Atlantic trade with the Americas, facilitated initially by Portuguese traders
trans-Saharan caravan routes from North Africa
direct migration of Yoruba communities from East Africa
questions.explanation: New World crops such as maize and cassava reached West Africa through the Atlantic trading networks established from the fifteenth century onward, introduced initially by Portuguese contact.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: Uthman dan Fodio launched the Sokoto Jihad in 1804 partly in response to
options: an invasion of Hausaland by the Bornu Empire
British demands for the abolition of the slave trade
perceived un-Islamic practices and oppressive taxation by Hausa rulers
the fall of the Oyo Empire
questions.explanation: Dan Fodio's movement grew out of grievances against syncretic religious practice and heavy, arbitrary taxation under Hausa kings, which he framed as departures from true Islamic governance.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The administrative unit at the head of each emirate within the Sokoto Caliphate was governed by an
options: Amanyanabo, elected by a council of chiefs
Attah, subordinate to the Obi of Onitsha
Oba, appointed directly by the Alaafin
Emir, who owed spiritual and political allegiance to the Sultan of Sokoto
questions.explanation: Each conquered territory within the Caliphate was reorganised as an emirate under an Emir who was appointed with a flag of authority (or 'flag investiture') from Sokoto and answered to the Sultan.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: Which of the following was NOT a major consequence of the Sokoto Jihad?
options: The extension of Fulani political control over much of Hausaland
A resurgence of Islamic scholarship and reform in the region
The immediate colonisation of Northern Nigeria by Britain
The establishment of the Sokoto Caliphate as a unified Islamic state
questions.explanation: British colonial conquest of Northern Nigeria came almost a century later, in the early 1900s, and was not a direct or immediate consequence of the 1804 Jihad.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: Bornu resisted incorporation into the Sokoto Caliphate largely due to the military and political leadership of
options: Muhammad al-Kanemi, who rallied Bornu's defence against Fulani jihadist forces
Usman dan Fodio's own son, Muhammadu Bello
Alaafin Abiodun of Oyo
the Emir of Kano
questions.explanation: Muhammad al-Kanemi organised effective resistance that preserved Bornu's independence from the expanding Sokoto Caliphate, eventually founding a new ruling dynasty there.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: A principal internal factor in the decline of the Old Oyo Empire in the early nineteenth century was
options: sudden loss of access to trans-Saharan trade routes
a succession of weak Alaafins and growing rivalry among provincial chiefs
military conquest by the Benin Kingdom
conversion of the Oyomesi to Christianity
questions.explanation: Old Oyo's central authority weakened as a series of ineffective rulers struggled to control ambitious provincial chiefs and generals, undermining imperial cohesion.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The revolt of Afonja, the Are-Ona-Kakanfo of Ilorin, against the Alaafin of Oyo is significant because it
options: opened the way for Fulani forces to seize control of Ilorin, extending the Jihad into Yorubaland
resulted in the total destruction of the Sokoto Caliphate
led directly to the founding of the city of Ibadan
ended the Atlantic slave trade in Yorubaland
questions.explanation: Afonja's rebellion against Oyo, in alliance with Fulani forces under Alimi, ultimately allowed the Fulani to take over Ilorin, turning it into an emirate and pushing jihadist influence into Yoruba territory.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Yoruba civil wars of the nineteenth century were fought most directly over
options: control of trade routes and political succession following the collapse of Old Oyo's authority
religious disputes between Islam and traditional religion
the introduction of British indirect rule
the abolition of the Atlantic slave trade
questions.explanation: With Old Oyo's central authority broken, rival Yoruba towns fought largely over control of trade routes, refugees and political dominance in the resulting power vacuum.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The city of Ibadan emerged during the Yoruba civil wars primarily as a
options: war camp that grew into a powerful, militarily organised city-state
trading post founded directly by European merchants
religious centre founded by Muslim clerics
colonial administrative headquarters established by Lagos
questions.explanation: Ibadan began as a war camp housing refugees and warriors from various Yoruba towns during the civil wars and grew into the dominant military power in Yorubaland.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Kiriji War (Ekiti Parapo War) of the 1880s was significant because it
options: resulted in the total destruction of Ibadan
marked the first contact between the Yoruba and European traders
was the longest and one of the last major wars of the Yoruba civil war era, ending largely through British mediation
led directly to the Sokoto Jihad
questions.explanation: The prolonged Kiriji War pitted Ibadan against an alliance of Ekiti, Ijesa and other states, and was eventually brought to an end partly through British-brokered peace efforts in 1886.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: Which of the following best describes the broader significance of nineteenth-century developments in the Nigeria area before formal colonial rule?
options: They were driven entirely by British colonial policy
They involved major political upheaval, including the rise of the Sokoto Caliphate and the collapse of Old Oyo's imperial order
They were a period of uninterrupted peace across all regions
They marked the complete disappearance of indigenous states
questions.explanation: The century before formal colonisation saw dramatic transformation across the Nigeria area, from the rise of the Sokoto Caliphate to the fragmentation of the Yoruba political order.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The abolition of the Atlantic slave trade by Britain in 1807 contributed to changes in Nigerian coastal economies by
options: causing the instant collapse of coastal city-states such as Bonny
triggering the Sokoto Jihad
encouraging a gradual shift toward legitimate commerce, especially palm oil exports
immediately ending all forms of slavery within Nigeria
questions.explanation: As Britain moved to suppress the Atlantic slave trade, coastal economies increasingly turned to 'legitimate commerce', particularly the export of palm oil, to sustain trade with Europe.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: King Jaja of Opobo rose to prominence in the nineteenth century largely through his efforts to
options: found the city of Ibadan during the Yoruba civil wars
lead the Sokoto Jihad into the Niger Delta
control the palm oil trade of the eastern Niger Delta and resist British commercial domination
negotiate the Berlin Conference on behalf of African states
questions.explanation: Jaja of Opobo built a powerful trading state around palm oil exports and resisted British attempts to bypass African middlemen, eventually leading to his deportation by the British in 1887.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Berlin Conference of 1884-85 is significant to Nigerian history mainly because it
options: laid down rules for European powers to formalise their claims to African territory, including Nigeria
established the Sokoto Caliphate
granted Nigeria its independence from Britain
abolished the trans-Atlantic slave trade
questions.explanation: The Berlin Conference set out principles for European powers to divide and claim African territories, providing the diplomatic framework within which Britain consolidated its claim to Nigeria.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Royal Niger Company, chartered in 1886, was significant chiefly because it
options: administered the Niger territories on Britain's behalf before direct colonial government was established
led the Sokoto Jihad
was responsible for granting Nigeria independence in 1960
organised the Aba Women's Riot
questions.explanation: Under Sir George Goldie, the Royal Niger Company exercised administrative and commercial control over the Niger territories under royal charter until the British government took over direct rule in 1900.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Amalgamation of the Northern and Southern Protectorates in 1914 was carried out chiefly to
options: reduce administrative costs and allow the wealthier South to help subsidise the North
unite all British West African colonies into a single country
grant immediate self-government to Nigerians
end the practice of Indirect Rule
questions.explanation: A key motive behind the 1914 Amalgamation, engineered by Lord Lugard, was financial: merging the two protectorates allowed revenue from the more commercially developed South to support the North.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: Under the policy of Indirect Rule, British colonial officials known as Residents were mainly responsible for
options: directly administering every village without involving traditional rulers
advising and supervising traditional rulers who retained day-to-day local administration
collecting taxes exclusively in Southern Nigeria
commanding British military garrisons only
questions.explanation: Residents served as supervisory advisers to traditional rulers, who continued to handle local governance, courts and tax collection under overall British oversight.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: Indirect Rule proved more difficult to apply successfully in south-eastern Nigeria than in the North mainly because
options: the Igbo refused all contact with British officials
Islam was already dominant throughout the South-East
many Igbo communities lacked the kind of centralised, hereditary chieftaincy the system assumed
the region had no economic value to the British
questions.explanation: Since Indirect Rule was designed around hierarchical monarchies like those in the North, its imposition on the more decentralised Igbo areas required the artificial creation of 'warrant chiefs', which caused lasting friction.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Warrant Chief system introduced in south-eastern Nigeria became a major source of grievance chiefly because
options: warrant chiefs were exempt from all colonial taxation
warrant chiefs were often seen as illegitimate outsiders imposed without traditional authority
the system was identical to traditional Igbo governance
warrant chiefs were elected democratically by their communities
questions.explanation: Because warrant chiefs were appointed by colonial officers rather than selected through traditional processes, many lacked genuine local legitimacy, breeding resentment that fed into unrest such as the Aba Women's Riot.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Ekumeku Movement, active among the Western Igbo (Anioma) into the early twentieth century, is best described as a
options: religious revival movement with no political aims
prolonged, largely guerrilla-style resistance against British colonial expansion
peaceful diplomatic negotiation with colonial officials
single, short-lived battle against British forces
questions.explanation: The Ekumeku Movement waged an extended campaign of guerrilla resistance over several decades against British attempts to impose colonial control on Western Igbo communities.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Anglo-Aro War of 1901-1902 was fought by the British mainly to
options: capture the city of Ibadan
break the political and religious influence of the Aro and the Ibiniukpabi oracle over south-eastern Nigeria
prevent the spread of Islam into the South-East
suppress the Egba Anti-tax Agitation
questions.explanation: British forces launched the Anglo-Aro Expedition to dismantle Aro power, particularly the authority wielded through the Ibiniukpabi oracle, which obstructed colonial penetration of the hinterland.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The 1897 British punitive expedition against Benin resulted directly in the
options: conversion of the Oba to Christianity
signing of the Berlin Treaty
immediate independence of the Benin Kingdom
exile of Oba Ovonramwen and the looting of the famous Benin Bronzes
questions.explanation: Following the killing of a British delegation, a retaliatory expedition sacked Benin City, exiled Oba Ovonramwen to Calabar, and carried off thousands of the kingdom's bronze and ivory artworks.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Satiru Uprising of 1906 near Sokoto is notable for combining resistance to British rule with opposition to
options: Christian missionary activity alone
the abolition of the slave trade
the introduction of Western education
the Sokoto Caliphate's own emirate authorities, whom the rebels also regarded as compromised
questions.explanation: The Satiru rebels, inspired by Mahdist beliefs, rose against both British colonial forces and the established emirate authorities they viewed as having submitted to colonial rule.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Egba Anti-tax Agitation of 1918 (Adubi War) arose principally from opposition to
options: the imposition of direct taxation and the erosion of Egba autonomy previously guaranteed by treaty
the founding of the University of Ibadan
British recognition of the Alake of Abeokuta
the introduction of Islam into Egbaland
questions.explanation: The Egba had previously enjoyed a degree of self-government under an 1893 treaty; the imposition of direct taxation and tighter colonial control sparked violent resistance in 1918.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Aba Women's Riot (Ogu Umunwaanyi) of 1929 was triggered immediately by
options: the appointment of a new British Governor-General
fears that a colonial census exercise signalled an intention to tax women
the introduction of Christianity to Aba
a dispute over palm oil prices
questions.explanation: When warrant chiefs began counting women, property and livestock, women interpreted this as preparation for extending taxation to them, sparking mass protests across the Owerri and Calabar provinces.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: A key long-term outcome of the Aba Women's Riot was that the British colonial government
options: replaced Indirect Rule with direct rule everywhere
immediately granted Nigeria independence
abolished all forms of local taxation nationwide
reformed the native court system and reduced the powers of unpopular warrant chiefs
questions.explanation: In the aftermath, the colonial administration commissioned inquiries and introduced reforms to the native administration and court systems in the East, curbing some of the warrant chiefs' powers.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: Which of the following pairs correctly matches a resistance movement with the region in which it primarily occurred?
options: Ekumeku Movement — Western Igbo (Anioma) area
Aba Women's Riot — Northern Nigeria
Anglo-Aro War — Egbaland
Satiru Uprising — Yoruba forest belt
questions.explanation: The Ekumeku Movement was centred among the Western Igbo (Anioma), while the other listed movements occurred in different regions than stated in the incorrect options.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: Overall, British colonial resistance movements across Nigeria between the 1890s and 1920s were generally provoked by
options: a single unified national leadership coordinating all revolts
British efforts to abolish traditional religion entirely
a shared desire among all groups to adopt Christianity
loss of political autonomy, unpopular taxation, and disruption of established economic and religious systems
questions.explanation: Though geographically scattered and locally distinct, these movements shared common grievances rooted in the loss of self-rule, new taxes, and disruption of pre-existing political, economic and religious structures.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The colonial economic policy of relying on Nigeria mainly as a source of raw materials and a market for British manufactured goods is best described as
options: a policy of full industrialisation designed to benefit Nigerians directly
an export-oriented, monocultural economic relationship serving imperial interests
a system of equal trade partnership between Britain and Nigeria
a deliberate strategy to make Nigeria self-sufficient in manufacturing
questions.explanation: Colonial economic policy generally oriented Nigeria's economy toward producing raw materials such as cocoa, groundnuts and palm produce for export, while serving as a market for British finished goods, with little investment in local industry.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The introduction of Western-style education in colonial Nigeria was pioneered largely by
options: the League of Nations
the Sokoto Caliphate's Islamic schools
the Royal Niger Company
Christian missionary societies operating mainly in the South
questions.explanation: Christian missions established most of the earliest Western-style schools in Nigeria, concentrated largely in the South, which contributed to regional disparities in Western education between North and South.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: Early Nigerian nationalist organisations such as the Nigerian Youth Movement (NYM) in the 1930s were primarily concerned with
options: negotiating the amalgamation of 1914
establishing a single unified Nigerian monarchy
demanding greater political representation and self-government for educated Nigerians
organising armed resistance against colonial forces
questions.explanation: The NYM, one of the earliest nationalist bodies, campaigned constitutionally for improved political rights, education and representation for Nigerians within the colonial system.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: Herbert Macaulay is widely regarded as a foundational figure in Nigerian nationalism mainly for his role in
options: commanding Nigerian federal troops in the Civil War
negotiating the Berlin Conference agreements
founding the Nigerian National Democratic Party (NNDP) and mobilising early political activism in Lagos
leading the Sokoto Jihad
questions.explanation: Herbert Macaulay founded the NNDP in 1923, one of Nigeria's earliest political parties, and is often described as the father of Nigerian nationalism for his pioneering political activism.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The National Council of Nigeria and the Cameroons (NCNC), formed in 1944, was significant because it
options: was formed exclusively to negotiate the 1914 Amalgamation
represented only the interests of the Northern emirates
was one of the first nationalist organisations to campaign on an explicitly national, pan-Nigerian scale
was a purely religious rather than political organisation
questions.explanation: Led initially by Herbert Macaulay and later Nnamdi Azikiwe, the NCNC sought to unite Nigerians and Cameroonians across ethnic and regional lines in pursuit of self-government.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: Nnamdi Azikiwe's contribution to Nigerian nationalism is particularly associated with his use of
options: the Sokoto Caliphate's religious authority
newspapers, especially the West African Pilot, to spread nationalist ideas
the Berlin Conference to challenge colonial claims
military force to expel colonial administrators
questions.explanation: Azikiwe built an influential press network, most notably the West African Pilot, which he used to popularise nationalist and pan-African ideas among Nigerians.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: Obafemi Awolowo's Action Group, formed in 1951, initially drew much of its early organisational base from the
options: Yoruba cultural association Egbe Omo Oduduwa
Nigerian Youth Movement's northern branches
Aro trading network
Sokoto Caliphate's emirate councils
questions.explanation: The Action Group grew substantially out of the Egbe Omo Oduduwa, a Yoruba cultural and political association that Awolowo had helped found to advance Yoruba interests.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Northern People's Congress (NPC), led by figures such as Ahmadu Bello, primarily represented the political interests of
options: Lagos-based professional elites
the Northern Region, emphasising caution toward rapid constitutional change
the Niger Delta trading states
the Eastern Region's minority communities
questions.explanation: The NPC was rooted in Northern Nigeria and, reflecting concerns about the North's relative underdevelopment in Western education, tended to favour a slower, more cautious approach to self-government.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Richards Constitution of 1946 is significant in Nigerian constitutional history mainly for
options: introducing regionalism by dividing Nigeria into three regions for administrative purposes
abolishing the position of Governor-General
establishing the First Republic
granting Nigeria full independence
questions.explanation: Governor Arthur Richards' constitution divided Nigeria into Northern, Eastern and Western regions, laying the groundwork for the regional structure that shaped later Nigerian politics.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Macpherson Constitution of 1951 is chiefly remembered for
options: introducing an expanded elected element and greater regional autonomy that intensified regional political rivalries
establishing Nigeria as a republic
abolishing regional government entirely
granting Nigeria independence outright
questions.explanation: The Macpherson Constitution broadened political participation and regional self-government, but its ambiguities also sharpened regional and party rivalries ahead of full self-rule.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Lyttleton Constitution of 1954 is notable for firmly establishing Nigeria as a
options: federation of three regions, each with substantial self-government
unitary state with a single central legislature
republic headed by an elected president
confederation of independent emirates
questions.explanation: The Lyttleton Constitution entrenched federalism in Nigeria, granting the three regions considerable autonomy while retaining a central government for matters of common concern.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: Nigeria attained full independence from Britain on
options: 1 October 1963
15 January 1966
6 July 1967
1 October 1960
questions.explanation: Nigeria became an independent nation on 1 October 1960, with Sir Abubakar Tafawa Balewa serving as its first Prime Minister.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: Sir Abubakar Tafawa Balewa's position at Nigeria's independence in 1960 was that of
options: Prime Minister, as head of government under a constitutional monarch
President, as head of a republic
Sultan of Sokoto, holding both political and religious power
Governor-General only, with no elected government
questions.explanation: At independence in 1960, Nigeria remained a Commonwealth realm with the British monarch as head of state, while Balewa served as the elected Prime Minister and head of government.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: Which of the following best explains why regionalism became such a dominant feature of Nigerian politics in the lead-up to independence?
options: The British insisted on a purely unitary government throughout the colonial period
Nigerian nationalists rejected any form of regional government
Regionalism was imposed suddenly at independence with no prior constitutional basis
Colonial constitutional reforms progressively devolved power to three regions, which came to be associated with dominant ethnic groups
questions.explanation: Successive constitutions from 1946 onward built up regional government structures, and because each region came to be politically dominated by a major ethnic group, regionalism and ethnic politics became deeply intertwined.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The 1953 Kano riots were significantly linked to tensions arising from
options: the Aba Women's Riot of 1929
a heated debate in the federal legislature over the timing of Nigerian self-government
disputes over the Amalgamation of 1914
the outcome of the 1959 federal elections
questions.explanation: The riots followed sharp disagreements between Northern and Southern politicians over an NCNC-Action Group motion demanding self-government by 1956, exposing deep regional divisions ahead of independence.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: Nigeria's transition from a monarchy to a republic in 1963 chiefly involved
options: replacing the British monarch as head of state with a Nigerian President while remaining a federation
merging the three regions into a single unitary state
ending all ties with the British Commonwealth
abolishing the federal system of government entirely
questions.explanation: In 1963, Nigeria became a republic within the Commonwealth, with Nnamdi Azikiwe becoming the first President as ceremonial head of state, while the federal structure was retained.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The January 1966 coup, Nigeria's first military coup, is often associated with the killing of prominent politicians including
options: Emperor Haile Selassie and Kwame Nkrumah
President Nnamdi Azikiwe and General Yakubu Gowon
Prime Minister Sir Abubakar Tafawa Balewa and Premier Ahmadu Bello
General Muhammadu Buhari and Chief Obafemi Awolowo
questions.explanation: The January 1966 coup, led by a group of mostly Igbo army officers, resulted in the deaths of several senior political figures, including Balewa and the Northern Premier Ahmadu Bello.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: General Yakubu Gowon came to power in July 1966 following a
options: referendum on Nigeria's republican status
peaceful handover from the departing colonial administration
counter-coup that removed General Aguiyi-Ironsi from power
popular election held after independence
questions.explanation: The July 1966 counter-coup, largely carried out by Northern officers, overthrew and killed Head of State General Aguiyi-Ironsi and brought General Yakubu Gowon to power.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The immediate political trigger for the declaration of the Republic of Biafra in May 1967 was
options: British pressure to divide Nigeria
the outcome of a national referendum on secession
Lt. Col. Odumegwu Ojukwu's response to communal violence against Igbo people and disputes over federal restructuring
a disagreement over the location of the federal capital
questions.explanation: Following the 1966 pogroms against Igbo people in the North and the breakdown of talks such as the Aburi Accord, Ojukwu declared the secession of the Eastern Region as the Republic of Biafra.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Nigerian Civil War formally began in July 1967 and ended in
options: January 1970, with the surrender of Biafran forces
October 1966, before Biafra was declared
1975, with the coup against Gowon
1979, with the return to civilian rule
questions.explanation: The Civil War concluded in January 1970 when Biafran forces, facing severe hardship, surrendered to the federal government, restoring Nigeria's territorial unity.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: Gowon's post-war policy toward the defeated Eastern Region was popularly summarised by the phrase
options: 'Unity in diversity'
'Peace at all costs'
'No victor, no vanquished'
'One nation, one destiny'
questions.explanation: Gowon's declaration of 'no victor, no vanquished' signalled an official policy of reconciliation rather than punitive treatment of the former Biafran territories after the war.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The creation of twelve states by the Gowon administration in 1967 was intended chiefly to
options: prepare for the transfer of the capital to Abuja
abolish federalism in favour of a unitary state
restore the pre-1914 regional boundaries
weaken the territorial base of Eastern Region secessionists and address minority grievances
questions.explanation: By breaking the three large regions into twelve states shortly before the war, Gowon aimed to undercut the cohesion of the secessionist Eastern Region and respond to long-standing minority demands for their own states.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: General Murtala Mohammed, who overthrew Gowon in 1975, is chiefly remembered for
options: negotiating Nigeria's independence in 1960
founding the Nigerian National Democratic Party
leading Nigeria into the Civil War
launching a vigorous anti-corruption drive and accelerating the transition programme to civilian rule
questions.explanation: Murtala Mohammed's short but impactful rule was marked by a purge of the civil service, anti-corruption measures and renewed momentum toward a return to civilian government, before his assassination in 1976.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Second Republic, inaugurated in 1979 under President Shehu Shagari, ended in December 1983 when
options: Nigeria became a one-party state
Shagari voluntarily resigned to make way for elections
the National Assembly dissolved the presidency
the military, led by Generals Buhari and Idiagbon, seized power in a coup
questions.explanation: The Second Republic was cut short by a military coup at the end of 1983, which cited widespread corruption and economic mismanagement as justification.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The annulment of the 12 June 1993 presidential election, widely believed to have been won by MKO Abiola, was ordered under the government of
options: General Olusegun Obasanjo
President Shehu Shagari
General Ibrahim Babangida
General Sani Abacha
questions.explanation: The controversial annulment of the June 1993 election took place under Babangida's military government, triggering a prolonged political crisis and widespread protest.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: Nigeria's return to civilian rule in the Fourth Republic began in 1999 with the election of
options: Olusegun Obasanjo as President
Sani Abacha as President
Ernest Shonekan as President
MKO Abiola as President
questions.explanation: Following General Abdulsalami Abubakar's transition programme, Olusegun Obasanjo was elected President in 1999, inaugurating the Fourth Republic that has continued since.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: Which of the following correctly places these Nigerian post-independence events in chronological order?
options: Second Republic; Independence; Civil War; January 1966 coup
Civil War; Independence; January 1966 coup; Second Republic
January 1966 coup; Civil War; Independence; Second Republic
Independence (1960); January 1966 coup; Civil War (1967-1970); Second Republic (1979)
questions.explanation: The correct sequence runs from independence in 1960, through the first coup in January 1966 and the Civil War of 1967-1970, to the Second Republic beginning in 1979.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Aburi Accord of January 1967, agreed between Gowon and Ojukwu in Ghana, ultimately failed mainly because
options: it was never actually signed by either leader
it was rejected outright by the British government
it called for the immediate independence of all Nigerian regions
the two sides disagreed sharply over how to implement its terms once back in Nigeria
questions.explanation: Although Gowon and Ojukwu reached an agreement on a looser federal structure at Aburi, differing interpretations of its implementation back home widened the rift that led toward civil war.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The ancient Kingdom of Ghana, which flourished well before the modern state of Ghana existed, built its wealth chiefly on
options: controlling and taxing the trans-Saharan gold and salt trade
exporting palm oil to Atlantic traders
controlling Red Sea maritime trade routes
mining diamonds for the European market
questions.explanation: Ancient Ghana's power rested on its strategic position controlling trans-Saharan trade routes, particularly the exchange of West African gold for Saharan salt.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Mali Empire reached the height of its fame in the fourteenth century under the ruler
options: Askia Muhammad, reformer of Songhai administration
Sonni Ali, conqueror of Timbuktu
Sundiata Keita, founder of the empire
Mansa Musa, renowned for his extraordinary pilgrimage to Mecca
questions.explanation: Mansa Musa's lavish 1324 pilgrimage to Mecca, during which he distributed vast quantities of gold, brought Mali international fame and put West Africa on medieval world maps.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The city of Timbuktu became famous across the medieval Islamic world chiefly as a centre of
options: Christian missionary activity
Islamic scholarship, learning and manuscript production
Atlantic slave trading
gold mining operations
questions.explanation: Under Mali and later Songhai rule, Timbuktu developed into a major centre of Islamic learning, home to renowned scholars, libraries and institutions such as the Sankore mosque-university.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Songhai Empire, which succeeded Mali as the dominant power in the Western Sudan, reached its territorial peak under
options: Mutapa rulers of south-central Africa
Shaka Zulu, who unified the Zulu kingdom
Mansa Musa, who founded the Songhai dynasty
Askia Muhammad, who expanded and reformed the empire's administration
questions.explanation: Askia Muhammad, who came to power after Sonni Ali, greatly expanded Songhai's territory and strengthened its administrative and religious institutions, marking the empire's golden age.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Songhai Empire's decline in the late sixteenth century was significantly accelerated by
options: the abolition of the trans-Saharan trade
internal conversion of the population away from Islam
an alliance between Songhai and European colonial powers
a Moroccan invasion equipped with firearms that defeated Songhai's traditional forces
questions.explanation: In 1591, a Moroccan expeditionary force armed with muskets defeated the larger but less technologically advanced Songhai army at the Battle of Tondibi, precipitating the empire's collapse.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Kanem-Bornu Empire's long historical importance in Central Africa rested substantially on its
options: control of key trans-Saharan trade routes and its role as a centre of Islamic learning near Lake Chad
role in the Zulu military system
domination of Atlantic coastal trade
position as the capital of the Mali Empire
questions.explanation: Kanem-Bornu's strategic location near Lake Chad allowed it to dominate important trans-Saharan trade routes for centuries while also developing as a significant centre of Islamic scholarship.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Great Zimbabwe civilisation of south-central Africa is best known for its
options: impressive dry-stone architecture and role as the centre of a major regional trading state
founding by European settlers
domination of trans-Saharan gold trade routes
conversion of its population to Islam
questions.explanation: Great Zimbabwe's remarkable dry-stone walled structures, built without mortar, testify to its role as the political and economic centre of a powerful state engaged in regional and long-distance trade, including gold.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The economy of Great Zimbabwe was significantly connected to long-distance trade in
options: palm oil exported to Europe
salt from the Sahara
cocoa exported to the Americas
gold and ivory exchanged with Swahili coast traders for goods such as Chinese porcelain and glass beads
questions.explanation: Archaeological finds of imported Chinese porcelain and glass beads at Great Zimbabwe confirm its links to Indian Ocean trade networks via Swahili coastal cities, exchanging gold and ivory for foreign luxury goods.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The trans-Atlantic slave trade, at its height from the sixteenth to nineteenth centuries, was driven primarily by demand for enslaved African labour on
options: gold mines in the Sahara
Islamic scholarly institutions in Timbuktu
trans-Saharan caravan routes
plantations in the Americas producing crops such as sugar, cotton and tobacco
questions.explanation: European colonial economies in the Americas relied heavily on enslaved African labour to work plantations producing lucrative export crops such as sugar, cotton and tobacco.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The trans-Atlantic slave trade's long-term effects on West African societies included
options: significant demographic loss and the disruption or transformation of existing political and social structures
the introduction of Islam to the coastal areas
the total elimination of indigenous states in the region
immediate and complete industrialisation of coastal economies
questions.explanation: The centuries-long trade caused substantial population loss in affected regions and reshaped political and social structures, as some states grew powerful through participation while others were destabilised.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The abolition of the trans-Atlantic slave trade by Britain in 1807 was enforced partly through
options: a naval squadron patrolling the West African coast to intercept slave ships
the immediate withdrawal of all Europeans from Africa
a treaty signed at the Berlin Conference
direct military conquest of African coastal kingdoms
questions.explanation: Britain deployed a naval squadron along the West African coast to intercept and suppress slave-trading vessels, though the trade persisted illegally for decades afterward.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Scramble for Africa refers to the
options: gradual withdrawal of European colonial powers from Africa after 1945
competition among African kingdoms for control of the gold trade
rapid colonisation and partition of the African continent by European powers in the late nineteenth century
expansion of the Sokoto Caliphate across West Africa
questions.explanation: In the decades following the Berlin Conference of 1884-85, European powers rapidly claimed and partitioned almost the entire African continent among themselves, a process known as the Scramble for Africa.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: Ethiopia's successful resistance to Italian colonisation at the Battle of Adwa in 1896 is historically significant because it
options: preserved Ethiopia as one of the few African states never colonised by a European power
led to the total colonisation of the whole Horn of Africa by Italy
marked the start of the Scramble for Africa
ended the trans-Atlantic slave trade
questions.explanation: Emperor Menelik II's decisive victory over Italian forces at Adwa secured Ethiopian independence, making it (along with Liberia) one of the only African states to escape formal European colonisation.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The wave of African independence in the late 1950s and 1960s is most closely associated with Ghana's independence in 1957 under the leadership of
options: Kwame Nkrumah
Nelson Mandela
Jomo Kenyatta
Julius Nyerere
questions.explanation: Ghana, led by Kwame Nkrumah, became the first sub-Saharan African colony to achieve independence in 1957, inspiring subsequent independence movements across the continent.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: Apartheid, the system of institutionalised racial segregation in South Africa, was formally dismantled in the early 1990s under the leadership largely associated with
options: Kwame Nkrumah and Julius Nyerere
F.W. de Klerk and Nelson Mandela
Jomo Kenyatta and Idi Amin
Haile Selassie and Menelik II
questions.explanation: The negotiated end of apartheid in the early 1990s, culminating in South Africa's first democratic elections in 1994, is chiefly associated with President F.W. de Klerk and Nelson Mandela.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The immediate event that triggered the outbreak of the First World War in 1914 was the
options: sinking of the Lusitania
signing of the Treaty of Versailles
invasion of Poland by Germany
assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria-Hungary in Sarajevo
questions.explanation: The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand by a Serbian nationalist in June 1914 set off a chain of alliance obligations that rapidly escalated into full-scale war.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Treaty of Versailles, which formally ended the First World War, is particularly notable for
options: creating the state of Israel
imposing harsh reparations and territorial losses on Germany
granting independence to African colonies
establishing the United Nations
questions.explanation: The 1919 Treaty of Versailles placed heavy financial reparations and territorial losses on Germany, resentments that many historians link to the later rise of Nazism.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The League of Nations, established after the First World War, ultimately failed to prevent renewed global conflict mainly because it
options: lacked an effective enforcement mechanism and the participation of major powers such as the United States
was replaced immediately by the United Nations
was too powerful and overreached its authority
focused exclusively on African affairs
questions.explanation: Without a standing military force and without the membership of key powers like the United States for much of its existence, the League proved unable to restrain aggressive expansion by states such as Japan, Italy and Germany.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Second World War in Europe is generally dated as beginning in September 1939 with
options: the attack on Pearl Harbor
the D-Day landings
Germany's invasion of Poland
the fall of France
questions.explanation: Britain and France declared war on Germany after its invasion of Poland in September 1939, marking the conventional start of the Second World War in Europe.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The entry of the United States into the Second World War in December 1941 followed directly from
options: the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor
the invasion of Poland
the D-Day landings in Normandy
the signing of the Treaty of Versailles
questions.explanation: Japan's surprise attack on the American naval base at Pearl Harbor in December 1941 led the United States to formally declare war, bringing it into the conflict.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Second World War in Europe formally ended in May 1945 with
options: the signing of the Treaty of Versailles
the atomic bombing of Hiroshima and Nagasaki
the unconditional surrender of Nazi Germany
the establishment of the United Nations
questions.explanation: Germany's unconditional surrender in May 1945, following the fall of Berlin, brought the European theatre of the Second World War to a close.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The United Nations was established in 1945 with a primary purpose of
options: managing the global gold standard
maintaining international peace and security and fostering cooperation among nations
administering the colonies of defeated powers only
replacing national governments with a single world government
questions.explanation: Formed in the aftermath of the Second World War, the United Nations was created chiefly to prevent future large-scale conflicts and promote international cooperation.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Cold War that developed after 1945 was characterised chiefly by
options: political and ideological rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union without direct large-scale war between them
open, continuous warfare between the United States and the Soviet Union
cooperation between the United States and the Soviet Union in colonising Africa
the reunification of Germany immediately after 1945
questions.explanation: The Cold War was defined by intense ideological, political and military rivalry between the capitalist West, led by the United States, and the communist East, led by the Soviet Union, but without a direct large-scale war between the two superpowers.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Berlin Wall, a key symbol of Cold War division, was constructed in
options: 1945, immediately after the war ended
1989, to mark German reunification
1919, following the Treaty of Versailles
1961, separating East and West Berlin
questions.explanation: East Germany built the Berlin Wall in 1961 to stop the flow of people from East to West Berlin, and it stood as a defining symbol of the Cold War until its fall in 1989.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Cold War is generally considered to have ended around 1991 following
options: the dissolution of the Soviet Union
the establishment of the League of Nations
the signing of the Treaty of Versailles
the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand
questions.explanation: The Cold War drew to a close with the collapse and formal dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991, ending decades of superpower rivalry.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: Which of the following best distinguishes the causes of the First World War from those of the Second World War?
options: Both wars were caused entirely by disputes over African colonies
Neither war involved any European powers
The First was caused by nuclear weapons and the Second by naval blockades
The First arose largely from alliance systems and imperial rivalries, while the Second was driven significantly by fascist expansionism and the failures of the Versailles settlement
questions.explanation: While the First World War grew out of a web of alliances and imperial competition among European powers, the Second was driven substantially by the aggressive expansionism of fascist regimes and unresolved grievances stemming from the Versailles settlement.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The United Nations, established in 1945, was created primarily to
options: maintain international peace and security and foster cooperation among nations
replace all national governments with a single world government
administer the colonies of defeated powers permanently
serve exclusively as a trade organisation
questions.explanation: The UN was founded after the Second World War with the central aim of maintaining international peace and security and promoting cooperation among member states.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The term 'Cold War' refers to the prolonged geopolitical tension mainly between which two blocs after 1945?
options: The United States and its allies versus the Soviet Union and its allies
China and Japan
Britain and France
Nigeria and Ghana
questions.explanation: The Cold War describes the decades-long ideological and geopolitical rivalry between the US-led Western bloc and the Soviet-led Eastern bloc following World War II.
